extracted.intended_audience: Applicants and recipient organizations (PD/PIs, AORs, institutional officials) for the NIH Director's Pioneer Award
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what happens after submission of an NIH Director's Pioneer Award application, including allowable post-submission materials, the two-phase peer review process, scoring, summary statements, pre-award/JIT requirements, funding deliberations, and pre-award negotiation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-submission materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Only documents to inform of unforeseen events, such as natural disasters, that substantially affect the ability to execute the proposed research will be accepted. No publication updates will be allowed as post-submission material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See NOT-OD-19-083 for more details. This is a strict limitation on what applicants may provide after submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review emphasis for Pioneer Award applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers will emphasize: the significance and innovation of the proposed project; the investigator's evidence for past innovation and the ability to commit effort that is sufficient for the proposed project; and a change in research direction that is not a logical extension or scale-up of ongoing efforts, motivated by a fundamental new insight prompting a new line of research or substantial departure from existing research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pioneer Award applications do not require preliminary data, specific aims, or a detailed research plan; reviewers therefore focus on transformative potential and investigator creativity rather than conventional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Scientific Review Officer (SRO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO is responsible for ensuring that each application receives an objective and fair initial peer review, and that all applicable laws, regulations, and policies are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties include analyzing application content and checking for completeness; documenting and managing conflicts of interest; recruiting qualified reviewers (considering authority in field, dedication to high quality/fair/objective reviews, collegiality, review experience, and balanced representation); assigning applications to reviewers for critiques and criterion scores; attending/overseeing administrative and regulatory aspects of peer review meetings; preparing summary statements; and serving as the point of contact for review-related questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase I (mail reviewers) composition & process
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase I is conducted by science area experts ('mail' reviewers) who submit independent assessments electronically and do not discuss applications with other reviewers. Two 'mail' reviewers are assigned based on the broad science areas chosen by the applicant; a third 'mail' reviewer has expertise outside the area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each mail reviewer provides scores and comments that are used in Phase II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase II (editorial panel) composition & process
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase II is conducted by an 'editorial panel' composed of scientists from an array of scientific backgrounds. Each application is assigned to three panel members and is not matched by area of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel members review applications from a broad viewpoint using mail reviewer comments, identify a subset (~25) of the most 'pioneering' applicants, and invite that subset for in-person or virtual interviews. Panel composition aims to capture wide breadth of expertise, experience, and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview evaluation focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The interview focuses on the qualifications and track record of the investigator, the broad impact potential of the proposed project, and the suitability of the proposal for the Pioneer Award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the interview, assigned reviewers provide a preliminary overall impact score and brief description. After the presentation and Q&A, the panel discusses the application and provides final scores; the panel discussion is summarized in the summary statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system and summary scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Each panel member privately scores discussed applications on a 1 (best) to 9 (worst) scale. The SRO averages the panel scores and multiplies the resulting number by 10 to yield an overall impact score (10 best to 90 worst).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel has access to full range of scores for discrimination among the select subset. These scores should not be compared to a regular R01 study section review. After the meeting, discussed applications receive an overall impact score within three business days via the PD/PI's eRA Commons account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Statement content and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Summary Statement prepared by the SRO will be available within 30 days of review. For discussed applications, it includes critiques from assigned editorial reviewers and a brief summary of the panel discussion. Applications not selected for panel interview are 'not discussed' and receive a summary statement with mail reviewer critiques but no editorial panel comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary statement provides valuable, but not exhaustive, feedback and will not contain every point reviewers found problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant response to Summary Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: PD/PIs of discussed applications may submit an optional two-page response to their summary statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The response may address reviewer issues and reinforce strengths but will not be seen by reviewers; it remains an internal NIH document used only by NIH staff during funding deliberations. The scientific contact will notify eligible applicants about response deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on contacting NIH staff after review
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have questions about your summary statement, contact the scientific contact listed in the funding opportunity. The scientific contact attends the review and may clarify panel discussion points or advise on funding probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contacting NIH staff to 'sell' your application or to express differences in scientific opinion related to reviewers' comments will not affect likelihood of funding. Best to email to schedule meetings so staff have time to review materials; be patient as responses may be delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-level review role (Council of Councils)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council of Councils assesses the first level of review for fairness and uniformity in the application of review criteria; it ensures the initial review was conducted with appropriate expertise, procedures, and without conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council is not tasked with reviewing scientific or technical merit and does not provide funding recommendations; it votes en bloc for concurrence with first-level recommendations. Applications must receive council approval to be eligible for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-award roles and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Key people during pre-award include NIH Staff (Grants Management Officer, Grants Management Specialist, Program Official) and recipient organization participants (Authorized Organizational Representative/Signing Official, PD/PI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GMO signs the Notice of Award and manages business/non-programmatic aspects; GMS supports day-to-day grant management; PO handles programmatic/scientific matters; AOR/SO certifies organizational compliance and accountability; PD/PI is responsible and accountable for conduct of project, submission of required reports, appropriate acknowledgment of federal support, and compliance with federal/organizational requirements. PD/PIs should maintain contact with Program Officer (scientific) and GMO (administrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Just-in-Time (JIT) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial peer review, NIH may request time-sensitive JIT information for applications within a competitive funding range. JIT is not a Notice of Award and should not be construed as an indicator of possible award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requested JIT information includes: Other support; Certification of IRB approval; Certification of IACUC approval; Human subjects training certification for all key personnel. JIT must be submitted for NIH review prior to award and may be submitted via the Just-In-Time function within eRA Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered in funding deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: Following review of all applicable information, NIH Office of the Director and the High-Risk, High-Reward Research program working group determine whether an award will be made. Considerations include: scientific and technical merit as determined by peer review (with consideration of PD/PI's optional response), availability of funds, conformance to clinical trial research policies, and relevance to programmatic priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic priorities include the potential for the investigator to lead groundbreaking and broadly impactful research despite inherent risks; unusually cross-cutting science; scientific balance in the portfolio; and potential to invigorate exceptionally innovative and impactful science broadly across the nation. Other NIH Institutes/Centers may fund meritorious applications that fit their missions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-award negotiation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-award includes negotiation between NIH and applicant organization when significant adjustments are required prior to award. NIH staff consider initial peer review recommendations (e.g., suggested changes to specific aims), overlap, level of effort, and Facilities and Administrative (F&A) costs during negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap review uses other support information to ensure no overlap with already funded projects (support, commitment, or budgetary). Program and grants management staff ensure sufficient levels of effort and apply negotiated F&A costs per the NIH Grants Policy Statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Award (NoA) significance and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The NoA is the legal document issued to notify the recipient that an award has been made and that funds are now available for the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NoA includes terms and conditions of the award, project start/end dates, funding amounts for current and future years, and contact information for the assigned Program Officer and Grants Management Specialist. NoAs are issued annually for each budget period and are contingent upon annual assessment of research progress and availability of funds. Communications about intent to award are not official until the NoA is issued.
